en: Oṃ. May there be well-being. Salutations to the illustrious Gaṇeśa. The Illustrious Bhairavī said: "O Mahādeva, having heard again and again this supreme expansion of the world, I am fulfilled, I am fulfilled, I am fulfilled; of this there is no doubt. Now I wish to hear the expansion of the world of Yama. Where indeed is the world of Yama, and how is it—below or even above? And where does a creature go when dead, having been brought under control by the nooses?

Where does the body dissolve, that corpse which is like a piece of wood? How many hells have been proclaimed, as well as the corresponding tortures? [Tell me] of the death of these people, the procedure for that time, and the ritual bathing for the deceased."

O Maheśvara, tell me also the ritual for the funeral rites of the gods, as well as the procedure for the final adornment and decoration; tell me of the removal of the corpse and the supreme ritual for the cremation ground. Why is there indeed a reversal [of status] for one who carries on foot that which was borne on the head? Why is the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) worn from the feet? O Īśāna, tell me the rule for the rites and the duties for ten days, O Lord. Tell me the destiny of men who are terrified by death itself. And regarding death, O Maheśāna, this recollection of yours is truly wonderful. Out of compassion, O Śambhu, speak for the sake of favoring the world. Śrī Bhairava:

O Goddess of Gods, even though the fickleness of the mind has been restrained, this supreme secret must not be told anywhere at all. It must not be given, O beautiful one, to the deceitful, the cruel, or those devoid of devotion; nor to the disciple of another, O Goddess of Gods, nor to one who neglects the conduct of the *samaya*, nor to one who mocks, nor to a reviler of the Vedas and Āgamas. However, O Great Goddess, this should undoubtedly be heard in an assembly by those who are devoted to the Guru, who follow the Vedas and Tantras, who are virtuous, equanimous in mind, and who observe the conduct of the *samaya*. It should be listened to with supreme devotion.

O beloved, this recollection of the truth of death from the mouth of the Guru should be completed from the first day following the passing of one’s father, mother, or Guru, up to the *dvādaśānta*. Whether heard or recited, it destroys even the greatest sins. It must not be heard through negligence, nor again in jest; otherwise, O Goddess, it brings obstacles to men—by this truth I swear to you. Having heard or recited it, one shall see neither Yama, nor the hells, nor the path of Yama, O Mistress of the Gods; such is the command of the Supreme Lord. Śrī Bhairavī said: Whether in the divine realm, the intermediate space, or the sky, above or across—tell me truly, O Maheśvara, where does the world of Yama reside?

Śrī Bhairava said: Listen, O Goddess, I shall describe the world of Yama, which is unsurpassed. To the south of the earth, both below and above, O Īśvarī, lies the world of Yama, declared to be beyond the netherworld (pātāla) and extremely difficult to traverse.

There dwell eighty-four hundred thousand and twenty-one hells, O Mistress of the Gods, which inflict torments upon sinners. Yama himself dwells right there, intent on the governance of the world. Citragupta also resides here, O Goddess, as the chief among the scribes (kāyasthas). Yakṣman, the best of those who hold the earth, dwells there eternally; all diseases, O Maheśānī, reside in the abode of Citragupta, causing fear.

Even for men who are great sinners, sages such as Vyāsa and others—great lords with vital energy drawn upward (ūrdhvaretas)—dwell in that abode of yours as judges of righteousness and unrighteousness. Yama is described as having large fangs, a staff in hand, and a mouth of fire; he is surrounded by Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, Vetālas, and Piśācas. He is eternally a source of terror to sinners and an increaser of honor for the virtuous. Before him stands Citragupta, with ink, a pen, and a ledger (karmapaṭṭī) in his hands; placing the ledger before him, he deliberates and records the good and evil deeds of both sinners and the virtuous. When a living being has died and is led to the house of Yama by his messengers...

Furthermore, having separately inscribed upon a leaf the nature of one's actions and sins, and having approached Yama facing him, he presents that leaf to Śiva. Upon that leaf, O beautiful one, the sages, having thoroughly reflected, write in their own hands with loud letters according to the rule: "In heaven or in hell, or among worms, insects, and moths, or likewise in the womb of animals, or even in the state of stationary beings—in such a place, at such a time, or for such a duration of time, let this person dwell, observing his own karma. Then Citragupta, taking that leaf from the assembly of sages, places it into the hand of Dharmarāja.
Furthermore, he commanded below that:
"Bring that great disease along this path—whether even or uneven, quickly or slowly—and bring him, whether he be a sinner or one free from sin."

O Goddess, in this way they lead the healthy man to the house of Yama, even though his accumulation of diseases might otherwise depart through medicines with great difficulty. For him whose affliction increases due to the exhaustion of his wealth, O Mistress of the Gods, one should perform religious merit for the sake of the next world; even a son, casting aside grief and weeping, should untiringly provide the provisions for the journey and the travel-baggage.

One should give cows, silver, gold, or various garments and vessels according to one's capacity. He who, while in good health, prepares there a collection of provisions for the journey, goes along that most difficult path happy and contented. O Great Goddess, he who, desiring to depart, performs the final gift for his own father preceded by the worship of Keśava, goes to hells, O Goddess, for as long as the fourteen Indras endure. Whatever gifts have been given by men themselves, all those indeed stand before him here. Then all his kinsmen, having abandoned their grief...

O Maheśvarī, they should repeatedly cause [the deceased] to remember the names of Viṣṇu and Śiva. O Mother of the World, O Bhuvaneśvarī, they should recite or cause others to recite hymns such as the Naraka-vināśana and others for one who has set out on the journey. A son, overcome with grief, should place the head upon the knees; for in ancient times, the cremation ground was ordained by Viṣṇu for the Daityas. Therefore, O Goddess, the placing of the head in front of the knees is prescribed. O beautiful one, seeing the head placed before the knees of the dying person, the spirits, ghosts, and piśācas flee in the ten directions. Thereafter, those who are undeluded should cause the great knowledge of Brāhmī to be recited, having heard which—

"By hearing this Great Vidyā, even a bound soul (paśu) is liberated from the fetters; by hearing it, a living being is released from tens of millions of great sins. Śrī Bhairavī said: "O Mahādeva, speak the truth out of a desire to show grace to the world—this Great Brahma-vidyā by hearing which a bound soul is liberated. O All-pervading Lord, tell me also, for the sake of my welfare, by what path the life-force (jīva) departs from the physical body."

"It kills ignorance, thus it is the Haṃsa"—by this Vedic statement, consciousness itself, having transformed into the vital breath (*prāṇa*), proceeds outward through the letter *ha* and enters again through the letter *sa*. "Haṃsa, Haṃsa, Haṃsa"—thus the living soul (*jīva*) constantly recites. [He is] seated in the pure place, the heart; he is the Vasu, whose form is splendor (*tejas*); he is the Hotṛ-priest who perceives all objects through the various doors of the senses. Śrī Bhairava said: "Listen, O Goddess, without weariness, to the supreme secret Brahma-vidyā, by hearing which a living being is immediately liberated from the state of a bound animal (*paśu*). [It is]: 'The Haṃsa, seated in purity, Viṣṇu, moving in the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*')."

I take refuge in the Vasu, the Hotṛ priest, the guest seated upon the altar, the dweller in the cave, the dweller among men, the dweller in the highest abode, the immortal, the one seated in the void (whether the space within the heart or the external sky), the lotus-born, the cow-born, the one born of truth, and the mountain-born. You alone are the pure; you alone are the awakened and stainless. (From the mother come skin, hair, blood, and flesh; from the father come sinews, bones, and marrow. Come, come! Recognize yourself and abandon this house of the six sheaths. For you are defiled by the three types of impurities: those pertaining to the deity, to māyā, and to the individual soul (āṇava).

Since you have fallen into impurity, therefore abandon conflict; since you have fallen into the state of a beast, deluded by the fetters of the body, therefore, having cast off your own beastly nature, come to your true nature. Just as a crystal gem becomes colored through contact with color, so you, abiding in the state of a beast, must now abandon that beastliness. O fortunate one, abandon delusion yourself within this worn-out body; abide in the supreme nature, stainless and having attained Buddhahood. Cast off that aged, wretched body enslaved by the fetters; you have fully attained your true nature—do not harbor delusion within the cage! (Oṃ 3) (Tāra-traya)

The letter *ha* joined with fire (*hrīṃ*), the letter *i* which is Māyā—O Goddess, at this moment of recitation, you are released from this bond of the noose; do not fall into delusion within this unreal cage. O Goddess, he who remembers this Great Brahma-vidyā at the time of death attains the state of Śiva, reaching which he does not grieve. What need is there for much speaking, O Mistress of the Gods? Remembering this Brahma-vidyā, one attains various siddhis that are difficult even for the dwellers of heaven to obtain. Since a man abandons the impurity of birth by breaking the power of Yama, how could there be fear of Yama for one who contemplates the Brahma-vidyā? Therefore, with every effort, [one should practice] this Brahma-vidyā.

O Maheśānī, the man who recites this or causes it to be heard shall attain union with Śiva. O Surasundarī, neither weeping nor sorrow is praised here; rather, the son and kinsmen should ensure that the dying person maintains mindfulness [of the Divine]. What is the use of that son, brother, father, or other relatives, if they do not cause the one about to die to remember the names of Śiva and Umā? As long as his breath remains, they should cause him to remember Śiva.

At the end of the breaths, the patient’s own sons and kinsmen should perform weeping and repeatedly utter cries of "Alas! Alas! while lamenting, O Goddess. When the life-breaths of the afflicted one depart upon the surface of the earth, gifts and other offerings should then be given, and the door to heaven must be opened. One should adorn the neck with garlands of Rudrākṣa beads and Tulasī, my dear; for upon seeing one wearing a garland of Rudrākṣas, O Maheśvarī, the messengers of Yama quickly flee in groups, suspecting him to be one of their own attendants. Now listen, O Queen of Gods, to the departure of the soul from the body, by knowing which one shall never again experience the suffering of birth. [The soul] contracts within...

Resorting to the state of the water of conscious knowledge (*citajñānoda*), the subtle atom—the Person (*puruṣa*) the size of a thumb—emerges from the center of the body, taking with it the aggregate of the senses like the wind carries the fragrance of a flower. Those who perceive subtle objects and see the subtle see this atom as it departs. Men are said to be of three kinds: superior, inferior, and middling. O Dear One, for the superior, [the soul] exits through the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*); for the middling, through the mouth; and for the inferior, O Maheśvarī, the life-force (*jīva*) departs through the anus. Having recognized that the Person has departed, one should perform a bath that removes impurities and ward off bodily ointments with warm water or even gentle [substances].

Then, one should cause the deceased to perform a ritual bath with mantras prescribed in the Vedas and Tantras, so that the vital functions (*prāṇavṛtti*) may be restored at the "gate of Brahman" (*brahmadvāra*). For that purpose, one should provide water for the feet and a sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*). Having caused him to put on two garments and fastened the sacred thread, one should apply the special clay from Gaṅgā, Prayāga, and Tulasī. O you who are worshipped by the gods, this immediately removes the sins accumulated since birth. Then, having perfumed this corpse of the deceased with fragrant substances and sealing its orifices, [one should proceed].

Having prepared incense along with pearls and the five gems, one should fill its mouth with that mixture. Seeing the body as equal to wood or a clod of earth, the pretas and piśācas enter through whatever openings there may be;

therefore, it must be covered with cloth so that the stability of the senses remains clearly fixed within the self through inward-turned consciousness, O Goddess. For this body is indeed the manifest form of Śiva and Śakti; just as it attains oneness, so too is the reversal [of suffering] achieved through the vehicle of the feet. One should adorn the body with garlands and then carry it to the forest amidst the ringing of bells.

Accompanied by the sounds of conchs, musical instruments, and the names of Hari, with Brahmins placed in front chanting the *Yama-gāthās*, one should reach the forest and cremate the body of the deceased— facing east— with pure sandalwood, *tulasī* wood, *aguru*, and *devadāru* wood, using both Vedic and Tantric mantras applied everywhere. Having cremated the corpse and wept profusely, the kinsmen should then assemble at an excellent sacred ford (*tīrtha*) for the burning of the hair and perform the supreme *tarpaṇa* (libation) with sesame seeds to bring satisfaction to the departed spirit.

One should kindle that fire which serves as the support for the living soul; when everything that is to be burned has been consumed without remainder, one should cast off the body. O Goddess worshipped by the best of gods, he who effects the liberation of the body in this manner attains eternal bliss consisting of union with Śiva, which is indeed certain. Thus has the liberation of the body for a living being—a bound soul (paśu) held in the grip of fetters—been described. O Mistress of the Gods, he who hears this at the ancestral cemetery (pitṛkṣaya) obtains both worldly enjoyment, liberation, and spiritual perfection (siddhi). Furthermore, O Goddess, having abandoned his former state, his father attains the state of Sadāśiva, freed from the six waves of affliction and all suffering. He returns [to his true nature].

Thus, there is no return from that state of Śiva to existence hereafter. Cold and heat belong to the body; greed and delusion belong to the mind; hunger and thirst belong to the vital breath (prāṇa); and hatred belongs to the senses.

[Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Liberation of Living Beings from the Body," in the description of the specific regions of Yama's world, within the section on the description of the worlds, in the *Śrī-Bhṛṅgīśa-saṃhitā*, during the dialogue between Bhairavī and Bhairava.]

Śrī Bhairava said: O Goddess of the gods, having taken the bones according to the requirements of place and time, one should perform the collection of the bones (*asthisañcayana*) on the fourth day, O beloved. Having returned home, the son, weeping along with his kinsmen, should then place the bones in secret within a corner of a storehouse. Having gone to a sacred bathing place (*tīrtha*), he should perform the rite of bathing with his clothes on. O Maheśānī, having bathed and then burned some grass, he should perform a circumambulation while reciting the Vedic mantra beginning with *agrayuṃṣi*, since this destroys the impurity arising from contact with a corpse. [He should smear the area] with cow dung, O Mahādevī...

One should smear one side of the hearth with [cow-dung], specifically the eastern and western portions; there, O Sovereign of the World, the son himself should cook the *caru*. Having cooked the *caru* there, O Sovereign of the World, he should add sesame, honey, milk, and urine in equal measure—half a *droṇa* [of each], O smiling Sovereign of the World. For one whose body is extremely emaciated and who is tormented by ghosts on the path, one should therefore thoroughly generate a well-nourished body through these substances. O beautiful lady, [the quantity] of milk, honey, sesame, and rice should be half a *droṇa* or even half of that.

Therefore, one should not make it deficient; having offered the nivāpa oblations, the son should offer the piṇḍas according to the mantra. Then, O Maheśānī, he should fill the two jars for the messenger and the deceased. Having placed the messenger’s jar around the jar of the deceased, O Maheśvarī, [he should proceed], because the messengers do not release the deceased even for half a moment. Taking the jar of the deceased, O Maheśvarī, he should place it on his left side at the entrance to the door. He should cause it to be set down in the intermediate space (antarikṣa) to the left, and nearby he should fix the tip of a branch from an auspicious tree, since the pretas and piśācas [dwell there].

O beloved Goddess of gods, because they always dwell upon the branches of the *agretara* tree which are bent downwards, they enter the house from that direction. Therefore, the daughter-in-law, having purified herself and become composed, should place a water-pot together with a lamp near the bones. O Great Goddess, when the deceased, the master of the house, and the deities see the water-pot, the deities residing in the house become agitated; being displaced from their stations, Carakī and the others emerge from the cremation ground. Since these deities were formerly worshipped by the performer [of the rite] when he had gone to the forest, they now cause agitation outside the house and obstruct auspicious rites.

With the left foot, one should cause the iron weapon (*lohāstra*) to enter within; likewise, with the right [foot], one should strike those spirits situated outside, such as stones and the like. O beautiful one, the Gaṇas stationed both inside and outside create obstacles for him who does not strike the multitude of spirits with the two weapons. Having slain the spirits with the weapon, one should indeed worship the water-pot (*sodakumbha*). O beautiful goddess, a *tila* oblation that destroys Rākṣasas must certainly be performed. O Mahādevī, in whichever place—whether on a riverbank, a stone, or even a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*)—one should perform it there for ten days. Because a person of deluded intellect wanders everywhere in all directions, [the rite should be done] in another location.

O beloved, even if his kinsmen perform the funeral rites, a man does not attain satisfaction even by the offering of hundreds of excellent oblations. One should utter the word "Preta" for both women and men; what is given with the word "Preta" brings joy to the deceased. For the sake of his gratification, Dharmarāja caused the Kumāreṣṭi sacrifice to be performed. O woman of excellent complexion, one should satisfy him with various substances—meats, fish, vegetables, mung beans, fruits, and roots.

O beautiful one, for him who does not worship the *kumāras*, obstacles shall arise at every step. Satisfaction of the *pretas* will not occur; therefore, a wise man should worship them. The *pūrṇa-pāraṇa* (the concluding meal) should be prepared by the kinsmen. That which is brought by those of the same lineage (*sagotra*) should be eaten together with the kinsmen. O beautiful one, they should sleep together until the end of the ten-day period. One should remember the virtues of the deceased and should not cause them to be disparaged. Those who sleep separately from the day of death for ten days—even if they are worthy of divine worship—will be born in the womb of a *preta*, experiencing misery even while living. Even if he is capable, he who does not offer the *pūrṇa-pāraṇa*...

O Śivā, for one who is still living, this is a source of nourishment; for one who is dead, it is as if they have entered hell. O Śivā, one should perform the *ārātrika* (lustration) rite with water over the funeral pitcher (*pretakumbha*). In whichever house, O Mahādevi, there is weeping or wailing for ten days, in that house the affliction of the deceased (*preta*) shall never arise. Where women, having come together from all sides, proclaim the virtues of the deceased with a single voice—that is known as pure weeping. Having heard [this],...

O Goddess of the Suras, the pleased pretas do not obstruct one's speech. For a preta who is afflicted by hunger and thirst and gazes at the door of one’s house, a loud sound must be made early every morning to subdue its burden. Śrī Bhairavī said:

"Having heard from the lotus of your mouth that the ritual extends for ten days, I am delighted, O Lord of the World, and I am repeatedly filled with bliss. Now, O observer of noble vows, I wish to hear the definitive rule regarding the *kanyā-śrāddha*, as well as the *cāturthika* and the *vālāvaṇa*. O Maheśvara, how should a daughter perform the funeral rites (*aurdhvadehika*) for her father or mother—should she do so with her husband’s wealth or with her own? Where does the body established by a *putrikā* (appointed daughter) enter and take its stand? Pray, sever this great doubt of mine out of a desire for my welfare. Śrī Bhairava said: "Listen, O Goddess, I shall explain."

Regarding the supreme rite for maidens, when the father or mother has died, it is declared that the period of impurity (*aśauca*) for the ancestors lasts three days. On the third day, one should perform the offering of ten funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*) and the water-libation (*udaka-kriyā*). On the fourth day, however, the daughter or her son should perform the *śrāddha* ceremony. Then, one should feed the Brahmins with fruits, roots, cooked foods, fish, meats, sweetmeats, various edibles, and cakes. Furthermore, the daughter's son should perform the *vaṇḍhudeva* [ancestral] rites for his maternal grandfather and grandmother.

Hika, even though she was still alive, entered the state of a departed spirit (preta). On the fourth day, however, by means of a *piṇḍa* offering of *lāvaṇa* provided by her granddaughters, the preta, now endowed with *lāvaṇya*, proceeded happily on his path.

Indeed, ghosts devour the body devoid of *lāvaṇya* on that path. In this regard, there is an illustration: just as dogs devour Devika—who was hunchbacked, poorly clothed, and deformed—so too do the spirits devour one who is bereft of *lāvaṇya*.
Regarding the eligibility for the *lāvaṇa-piṇḍa*, it is certain that it is due to affection for the gods, whether the daughters were given away in marriage or not.

O Maheśvarī, in the Cāturthika rite, some wealth must be given by the brother himself; otherwise, the gift of the daughter (kanyādāna) shall not be lost even upon death. A body prepared for a Putrikā resides in the city of Mahāraudra.

A body prepared for a son remains as a ghost on the path, afflicted, emaciated, wasted away, and decrepit, O beautiful goddess. Having reached the region of Raudrapura and being joined with that decrepit state, it goes to the abode of Yama through union with the body of a Putrikā. Therefore, with every effort, one should perform the funeral rites (aurdhvadehika) for the parents as a Putrikā, O beloved, which brings about nourishment and prosperity even after their death, provided she is capable when her parents have passed away.

If one does not perform the funeral rites (*aurdhvadehika*), one attains the hell of the dead; one becomes a lizard, a house-lizard, or a two-faced creature, O Goddess, and is born indeed as a pauper. While in the state of a ghost (*preta*), there is no satisfaction in the most difficult realm of Yama. O Goddess, one should perform the rites for the parents without laziness according to the previously mentioned procedure. The ritual for the attainment of the *preta*-body lasts for ten days. Having reached the tenth day, O Mistress of the Gods, one should perform the shaving of hair at a sacred ford (*tīrtha*). For the sake of liberation from grief, O Goddess, one should cut the nails and hair. Having performed this and having bathed, one should place the *preta*-vessel upon the left shoulder and recite the mantra in the unfathomable [depth], O Maheśāni.

One should again perform the ritual bath and, having gone to the riverbank, wash one's garment. The removal of the garment should be performed by one's own kinsmen in the northeast direction, because in times of grief the appearance of people's garments becomes soiled; therefore, O Goddess, the kinsmen should provide a new appearance. Any kinsman who does not give a garment or the value of a garment becomes like a lion [in its ferocity] toward the deceased, and once dead, he experiences hell.

O Great Goddess, he who does not himself deliver his own kinsman from sorrow certainly enters the state of a *preta* until the dissolution of all beings (*ābhūtasaṃplava*). O Goddess, having entered a body that lasts for ten days, that person (the *jīva*) becomes hungry, repeatedly beholding the door while weeping, with a mouth parched by thirst, O Maheśī. Then, at dawn, one should cook a sacrificial oblation (*caru*) with milk, honey, clarified butter, guggulu, moist fruits, various roots, and cloths; and one should feed [the *preta*] with it.

Those who, at dawn on the second day, perform the *anvaśrāddha* for the deceased according to their capacity—whether for the sake of providing rest on earth, for the removal of thirst, or out of devotion to bring constant happiness to the departed person—such a man attains vast enjoyments even while living, and though dead, shall go to the abode of the gods. After the offering of water-libations (*jalāñjali*), the dismissal of the deceased (*pretavisarjana*) is performed with wooden sticks;

then, O Daughter of the Mountain, all stones must be cast away. Thus, O Īśānī, the ritual procedure lasting up to ten days has been declared to you; when heard or recited with devotion, it grants all perfections.

[Thus ends the second chapter, on the Recollection of the Reality of Death, in the Bhṛṅgīśa-saṃhitā. Śrī Bhairava said: O Īśvarī, having bathed according to the prescribed rites at the clear and pure dawn, and having worshipped the jar (kalaśa) and Viṣṇu, one should then worship the water-jars with gems, food offerings, and their respective appurtenances, using thirteen types of verses.

Then, O Maheśānī, one should honor the Brāhmaṇas with various kinds of foods to be chewed and eaten, such as *bakarbaras*, *vaṭakas*, drinks, fruits, and roots; with *ghṛtapūras*, *modakas*, and the five types of cooked sweets;

and with fish, meat, and cakes that satisfy the departed (*pretas*), O beloved—feeding the Brāhmaṇas with devotion according to the extent of one's own wealth. One should not distress oneself for the sake of wealth, O Goddess, nor should one neglect the Dharma.

Having carefully considered both material wealth and spiritual merit, one should perform various acts of giving; and having understood the place, the time, oneself, the object given, the purpose of the gift, its origin, and its current state, one should carry out the action.

What is given to an unworthy recipient leads one to heaven, while what is given to an unworthy recipient leads toward hell. Cows, bulls, horses, and likewise beds—these gifts should ultimately be offered for the deceased according to one's means. Alternatively, one should perform the *vṛṣadharma* (the rite of the bull) for the deceased, which grants liberation. O dear one, one should perform the *vṛṣotsarga* (the release of a bull) in accordance with the place and time; otherwise, by performing the *vṛṣadharma* without considering the place and time, one would attain hell. [One should honor] the Brahmins with devotion according to the prescribed rules.

He who worships and feeds [the Brahmins] attains proximity to Śiva, reaching which he no longer grieves. One should present water-pots along with clothes and food to the Brahmins; having dismissed the Brahmins, O Goddess, with prostrations and requests for forgiveness, one should then perform the *sapiṇḍana* on the twelfth day. Because family customs are infinite and because of the uncertainty of death, everything should be performed by dismissing [the rites] and performing the *sapiṇḍana* on the twelfth day.

Thus has this been told to you, O Mother of the World: the *śrāddha* joined with the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, whether on the eleventh or the twelfth day, O Goddess, liberates one from the state of being a ghost upon hearing it on the twelfth day.

When his life is exhausted, O Goddess, this man is bound with nooses by the servants of Yama and led away—like a dog or a monkey—wailing "Alas! Alas! in despair, remembering his sons, grandsons, and family, overwhelmed by delusion.

On that most terrible path of Yama, he cries out repeatedly and helplessly, again and again: "What shall I do? Where shall I go? I find no moment of rest; where is my home? Where are my son and wife?"

"Where is my wealth and grain? Where are my possessions? And where are all my friends, relations, and kinsmen? Where must I go, destitute and as if struck down, upon a path devoid of shade, cold, and full of many hardships? Where shall I go alone, without kin? What kind of state is this? Lamenting thus, he proceeds toward the abode of Yama. Seeing the weeping deceased, those cruel sons violently beat him on the path with pestles.

Then, with iron clubs and shouts of "Huṃ!", they say to the preta: "O you of evil mind, why do you weep? In this land of Bhārata, this field of action so difficult to attain, why did you not perform virtuous deeds? Why do you weep, O you of evil mind?

No gift was given, no oblation offered into the fire, no austerity practiced, and no liberation for the deceased performed. No bath was taken at a sacred ford, no worship of Hari was done; your human birth has passed in vain today. No service was rendered to your parents, nor was even a single cowrie shell offered in sacrifice to the gods."

"O fool, why do you weep now as you depart? Why did you not offer food into the mouths of the brāhmaṇas, O enemy of men? Why did you, a great sinner, constantly perform only obligatory rites and never occasional ones?

Why have you committed sin like honey, O deluded one? Why do you go away lamenting now? Did you not drink the water from Viṣṇu’s feet here? Did you not hear the Bhāgavata narrative? Did you not cultivate the company of the virtuous? Or did you not meditate upon the pair of the Lord’s lotus feet?"

"O fool, you sinner! Why did you not visit holy places such as the Gaṅgā and Prayāga? O great fool, why do you weep? Having obtained this human birth so difficult to attain, why was no merit performed by you, whose intellect was distracted by delusion? Why is the path to the world of Yama—so terrible for sinners and so difficult to cross—not yet heard of by you? Having thus rebuked that ghost in many ways, O beloved, the messengers strike him with clubs and drag him away with nooses.

O Goddess, those who travel on such an extremely difficult path, encountering various afflictions and tormented by distress along with throngs of departed spirits, should perform a *śrāddha* at intervals to dispel the fatigue of the journey.

A son who observes celibacy (*brahmacarya*) should provide a water-pot and offer a lamp daily to destroy the darkness. By feeding Brahmins according to his desire, he shall become a vessel for prosperity. This applies to the daily *śrāddha*, O Queen of the Gods.

O Maheśāna, a celibate (brahmacārī) who has conquered his senses obtains, in particular, the fruit of the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice. Whatever man in this world should falter from celibacy, those [deities] cause him to drink his own semen after he has become a ghost (preta). Therefore, O Lord of Devas, a Brahmin who performs [the rite] as a celibate with conquered senses shall obtain the fruit of the Jyotiṣṭoma. Śrī Bhairavī said: O Maheśāna, in this Kali age, no one...

O observer of excellent vows, how can the path of the journey to Yama—which is difficult to endure due to its weariness—be equal to that of one who has conquered his senses, is firm in his observances, or maintains celibacy, yet remains unfulfilled in performing the daily *śrāddha* for his parents?

O Bhava, whether due to calamities of place and time, or even because of poverty, how can the path to Yama be a source of happiness for the deceased? Śrī Bhairava said: Listen attentively, O wise one, to this question.

O Goddess of the Asuras, the wise one, having performed the ritual bath according to the rules upon rising in the morning, should offer libations to the deceased every day for a period of twelve days up to one year using a vessel made of copper. O Śivā, by means of this libation from a water-pot, one obtains that same fruit which results from the ritual gift of a thousand tawny cows at Kurukṣetra, Prayāga, or the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean; wherever the deceased may go on the path of the journey to the other world, [he is satisfied].

O Goddess, one who is afflicted by thirst should drink the water from the jar at every moment and in every place. O Mistress of the Gods, I shall now describe the provisions for the journey (*pātheya*) that brings satisfaction to the departed spirits (*pretas*). O Mother of the Universe, having risen in the morning and bathed, one should smear the ground with cow-dung and cook *caru* there for the sake of the departed. O Īśvarī, because this *caru* is prepared day after day for the sake of the departed, it is called "provisions for the journey" (*pātheya*). O Mother of the Universe, one should perform worship for the sake of the departed.

O Maheśvarī, one who performs *cāndrāyaṇa* and *kṛcchra* penances shall obtain their fruit through this alone. O Goddess of Devas, O Śivā, he who, while healthy, does not perform the worship of the deceased (*pretārcana*) goes constantly and in many ways to twenty-one different hells. O beautiful one, with devotion and with his whole being, one should diligently place a lamp-wick soaked in ghee on the path of Yama, which destroys the darkness [of ignorance]. O lady, he who does not offer a lamp-wick for the sake of the deceased will find his own path [obstructed].

Otherwise, by an improper method, at every step, that performer shall become blind as a ghost in birth after birth. While the water from the jar, the arghya-offering, and the lamp are being offered in sequence, they should utter the name of the deceased, accompanied by the proclamation of his lineage (*gotra*).

O Goddess, if one should constantly give even this much as the traveler’s provision (*pātheya*) for the deceased soul, he obtains eternal happiness through that blessing; there is no doubt or hesitation in this matter. Śrī Bhairavī:

A great doubt wanders extensively within my heart, O Śambhu; O Īśāna, how could anyone other than you have the power to sever it? Regarding the funeral rites performed on the tenth day, those accumulations of *piṇḍas* which are offered for the sake of the deceased’s bodily perfection as he travels the path of death—by which specific ones are his various limbs nourished and made whole? O Lord of the Universe, tell me this in its entirety. Śrī Bhairava said: Listen, O beautiful one.

Out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds, I shall explain the determination of that supreme and most wonderful secret which you have asked: O Śivā, by the first *piṇḍa* (funerary offering), the head of the dying person is formed; by the second, the ears, eyes, and nose are formed in brief;

by the third, the neck, mouth, arms, and chest are formed in due order; by the fourth *piṇḍa*, the navel, genitals, and anus; and by the fifth, the thighs, shanks, and feet are formed in their entirety.

By the sixth [day] all the vital points (*marmāṇi*) [are abandoned], by the seventh the channels (*nāḍyaḥ*); by the eighth the teeth and tongue; and by the ninth, vitality (*vīrya*). By the tenth, there is fullness, satiety, and the cessation of hunger. In this sequence, O Goddess of the Gods, the embodied soul finally offers up the material body among the five elements and enters the physical frame born of a womb. Suffering the pain of hunger, thirst, and the like while traveling on the path, it gazes toward the door of the house.

Day after day, the deceased travels two hundred and forty *yojanas* in seven days and nights. Bound by nooses and crying out "Alas! Alas! repeatedly, having passed sixteen excellent cities along the way, that deceased one proceeds in due order toward the city of Yama according to his auspicious and inauspicious deeds. [Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Ritual for Worshipping the Deceased," in the *Śrī Bhṛṅgīśasaṃhitā*, within the section on the Recollection of the Reality of Death.]

Bhairavī said: "Now I wish to hear the characteristics of the path of Yama; what is its nature in form, and how great is it in measure? Bhairava said: "Listen, O Goddess, to the description of the path of Yama, which is cruel and constantly causes suffering to sinners, both in its appearance and its extent. In some places it is strewn with heated sand, in others it is covered with needles; in some parts it is made of iron, and in others it is crowded with a multitude of sharp thorns."

It is inhabited by trees upon which the blades of weapons fall every moment; it is defiled by mice with gnawing teeth and by worms; and it is pervaded by snakes, pythons, and scorpions of virulent poison, which bite out of anger those sinful worlds that are difficult to endure. In some places it is frequented by gadflies, lice, and flies; it is occupied by flocks of crows with iron beaks, by vultures, by *cilla* birds, and by lions and leopards.

O Lord of Gods, [the place] was filled on all sides by boat-like beings with tusks like iron, by most terrible owls, and by dogs with hideous faces; by the messengers of Yama with iron fangs and iron mouths;

by those of massive bodies, tawny eyes, long shanks, and terrifying forms; by those with eyes on their heads, tongues reaching to their collarbones, and rolling pupils; by those vomiting fire from their mouths and intent on loud, boisterous laughter—a great clamor that rendered one deaf.

O beautiful lady, that most dreadful path we must travel is filled with such messengers dispatched here and there by Citragupta—frightening the hosts of pretas as they seize them by the legs, causing great distress; these messengers, equipped with various weapons, intent on clapping their hands, and repeatedly stamping their long feet so as to shake the earth. Enveloped in terrible darkness and fraught with manifold perils on all sides, there is no shade from trees anywhere to provide relief from the intense heat, where a creature might find rest for even a moment.

O Goddess of the gods, when thirst increases, there is no reservoir of water anywhere; for embodied beings here, dharma alone is the refuge. This great path, measuring eighty-six thousand yojanas in extent, is said to be impassable for those of sinful deeds. Therefore, with every effort, a wise person should practice dharma alone. Dharma is indeed one's companion everywhere, providing freedom from fear from all sides. Neither father, nor brother, nor friend, nor kinsmen; neither son, nor grandson, nor wealth, nor wife, nor houses—O Goddess of the gods, these will not carry even a single step of that person. Only one being travels here, accompanied by dharma as his companion.

Having attained this human birth in this auspicious land of Bhārata, and knowing that everything is indeed impermanent, one should practice only dharma. One should perform the duties of the afternoon in the forenoon; there should be no delay here, for time wakes up like a leaf-fall. O Goddess, while the body is healthy, while the senses have not yet decayed, and before it is shattered by old age and falls to the earth—during that very time, [one must act] by people.

O Mother, one should perform the task of self-protection before the terrifying Yama arrives with noose in hand; for a person who is deluded, it is like a blind man striking with his hand. Therefore, desiring one's own welfare, one should practice what is beneficial at that very time.

As long as this house of the body is healthy, as long as there is no decay of life, as long as the power of the senses is unimpeded, and as long as old age is far off, so long should a wise person exert effort toward their own spiritual welfare.

O Goddess, what kind of effort is this, like digging a well even while one's house is in great flames? Thus have I described to you, O Goddess, this terrifying path of the wicked; tell me always, what more do you wish to hear?

Śrī Bhairavī said: O Śaṅkara, having heard of this most difficult path to the world of Yama, my body trembles like a creeper shaken by a powerful wind. O Supreme Lord, I am terrified, for it is covered with protruding thorns.

O Lord of Gods, tell me: how many resting places are there for a living being? Tell me where a creature, though bound by fetters, might rest for even a moment; and if, lacking such rest, he must indeed go on day and night, in what region and at what spots does he find respite?

Śrī Bhairava, distressed by the exhaustion of the journey and desiring to show grace to the worlds out of compassion, said: "Listen, O Varārohā, I shall describe those places where a living being may find rest on the terrifying path of Yama, O Goddess, Mistress of the Gods. For thirteen days, the deceased, bound by the fetters of the Lord of Death, having uttered many *huṃ* sounds, takes refuge in the shade of a banyan tree on the bank of the Puṣyabhadra river. Remembering his home, his wife, his sons, and his grandsons, O Maheśvarī, he weeps there again and again, parched with thirst and tormented by hunger. Hearing the piteous words of the creature as he laments repeatedly—"

The messengers of Yama, with cruel faces, spoke as they struck him. The messengers said: "O fool, you must certainly go upon the path crowded with ghosts, where there is no market, neither buying nor selling. Traveling that path, you shall experience whatever karma you have earned. Now, O fool, what is the use of these vain lamentations? Even while they were speaking thus and striking him severely by the hundreds, O beautiful one, whatever little was given by his sons during the monthly *śrāddha*—whether out of affection or compassion—he does not eat it. There, O Queen, seeing a moving being named Rājanimīśvara, he [sees] the monthly *piṇḍa*..."

Without questioning, the deceased shall go to the city of Sauri. There, having eaten the *śrāddha* offering consisting of sweet food and salt given by his own kinsmen during the third fortnight (*trimāsika*), he passes beyond that city and goes to the abode of the Lord of Men (*Narendra*). There, seeing the hosts of *pretas*, he becomes terrified and laments.

(The gift of musk and betel) Having eaten the *piṇḍa* offered there during the second month (*dvimāsika*), O Great Goddess, he proceeds while bound with nooses and being beaten by wicked guards. (The gift of a ring, milk, rice, cotton, and silk cloth) After five fortnights, O Maheśānī, he reaches the gentle city.

O Beloved, even there one may encounter various torments inflicted by the messengers of Yama; O Great Goddess, having partaken of the *śrāddha* offering, one then departs. (The gift of a water-pot and gold: In the third month, one dwells in the auspicious city of the Gandharvas.
[One cries out: "Eat the third-month *piṇḍa*! and thus one leaves the high mountain. Parjanya...

O Goddess of the Gods, having received the *cāturthika* offering (the gift of a stool and a wooden ladle) poured upon his head by his kinsmen in the fifth month, the deceased spirit, considering it a *śrāddha*, resorts to the city of the cruel Yama. Having eaten and rested for a *nāḍī* (twenty-four minutes), he is growled at by the servants of Yama and, afflicted by hunger and thirst, O Maheśvarī, he departs for the City of Citra. There, O beautiful lady, having asked the King named Vicitra, and having eaten the *piṇḍa* offered in the fifth month (less than six months), [having received] the gift of a cow, a ring, a boat, an umbrella, and so forth, he goes to the bank of the river. "Who is my son? Who is my kinsman? [he cries]. *(Salutations to Śrī Gaṇeśa)* In the fifth month, O Goddess, that which is given by his own kinsmen—[the gift of] a water-vessel, sandals, and so forth—the deceased spirit, having consumed it and rested for a *nāḍī*, is reviled by the messengers of Yama. Afflicted by hunger and thirst, O Great Goddess, he proceeds to the wondrous city. There, O lovely one, having inquired of the King named Vicitra and having partaken of the *piṇḍa* offered in the fifth month (or less than six months)—[receiving] a cow, a seal-ring, a boat, an umbrella, and other gifts—he goes to the riverbank. "Where is my son? Where is my relative? [he asks].

"Or perhaps a heart-friend who will deliver me from this ocean of sorrow? Wailing repeatedly and being beaten by the servants, [he asks: 'O mother, why have you brought this son of yours to this great river?'"

"Is there any provision for the journey here by which you shall cross this river? Fishermen dwell here who strike [beings] by the thousands; O fool, [cross] this difficult-to-traverse river of the hungry ghosts (preta), which has swallowed you! Thus threatened there by those with their lips bitten, he falls from the sky to the ground upon seeing the terrible Vaitaraṇī river. Having eaten there the funeral ball (piṇḍa) offered for six months—[specifically the gift of molasses, rice, and wheat flour]—the hungry ghosts depart. Having crossed that river with difficulty, one should go to the city of many calamities; many fall away, and many perish.

O beautiful one, having consumed the seventh-month rice-ball (*piṇḍa*), the preta resorts to the city of Trapuṣa, which brings suffering; there, the pretas torment him with great agonies. Having eaten the eighth-month rice-ball, he goes to the city of Ghurghura, which is filled with the clamor of the cries of suffering from the world of pretas; his ears being deafened by that noise, O auspicious lady, he trembles excessively. But having consumed the ninth-month rice-ball, he shall go to the city of Tapta, where, being intensely tormented by fire, he remains in extreme distress.

O beloved, thinking that the funeral cake (piṇḍa) for the tenth month has been offered, one who licks oneself with sharp claws out of suffering enters the city of Raudra, where hungry ghosts (pretas), craving flesh, search for them like wolves. Having eaten the cake given by their own kinsmen in the eleventh month, [the donor of an umbrella] enters the city of Parjanya, where clouds rain down hailstones and thick mist, covering the hungry ghosts day and night so that their scabs and wounds are healed. Thinking that the cake for the year-deficient (ūnābdika) has been offered in the city of Parjanya, he then proceeds to the city of the gods.

The city named Śiprīṃśitā (the Gift of Garments and Blankets) is forty-four yojanas in extent. It has four gates, O Goddess of the Gods, and is frequented by Siddhas and Cāraṇas. It resounds with the humming of bees amidst various blooming flowers. There, one whose limbs have shriveled on all sides due to the force of harsh cold, who is fleeing in all directions and whose vision is obscured by frost, stands about weeping aloud, repenting for his own past deeds. Assuming great wretchedness, he proceeds toward that city of Yama.

It was filled with gardens containing trees that provided cool shade and bore fruit; it was supplied with water-channels and adorned with young grass and tender shoots. It was graced by beautiful houses built of golden bricks, featuring most delightful gates made of sapphire and lapis lazuli. Its pathways were perfumed by the smoke arising from burning aloe-wood. In its center, O Goddess, was the vast Saṅjavana garden, constructed of crystal stones and unadorned by crowns, yet [beautified] by lotus-gems.

It was adorned with a protective covering at its extremities, filled with various enjoyments, and presided over by celestial women. O Śivā, the sound of singing Gandharvas rising upward was pleasant to hear; at every door stood attendants bearing canes, adorned with various ornaments, graced by their exquisite beauty. Standing there in the inner courtyard, free from weariness, he worshipped the excellent sages such as Vyāsa who were stationed all around on a throne made of jewels. O Goddess, Yama stood there holding his staff and bearing a serpent resembling a noose, while Citragupta...

He constantly delighted the minds of the ministers and the courtiers with auspicious words of grace; he was terrifying to sinners deluded by their own evil deeds, yet his form appeared gentle to virtuous people as he bestowed gifts upon them.

In that region, various terrible diseases such as cholera and others, assuming distinct and horrific forms, reside in the abode of Citragupta as his diverse messengers, acting according to his commands. O Maheśvarī, when one has died, they are led through the southern gate by the servants of Yama. There are eighty-four lakhs of hells, O Goddess, and among them, twenty-one are particularly dreadful: Tāmisra, Lohaśaṅku, Mahāraurava, Śalmali, Raurava, Kuṭmala, and Pūtimṛttika.

The Skeleton-String, the Mass of Corpses, the Iron Vessel, the Poisonous, the Intense Heating, the Great Hell Kākolī, Sañjīvana, Mahāpatha, Avīci, Andhatāmisra, Kumbhīpāka, and likewise Asipatravana—these twenty-one hells are situated here; listen, O beloved one! Śrī Bhairavī said: O Lord, this river called Vaitaraṇī, which was mentioned in the middle of the path of Yama, is difficult for those of evil deeds to cross.

O Lord, O Master, please describe to me in detail those hells according to their true nature as established by authoritative means; who, by what actions, sink into them; and by what means those humans obtain liberation from them—tell all that to me, O Auspicious One.

Śrī Bhairava said: O Goddess, hear now the nature, the dimensions, and the extent of this great river named Vaitaraṇī at my southern gate. It is rich with waters of pus and blood, teeming with serpents and scorpions, and strewn on all sides with hair, moss, bones, and small stones. With its violent current, it instantly sweeps away even mountains; it is enveloped by the intensely hot flames of Mahākālāgnirudra, which, resembling mountain peaks, collide with one another.

O Goddess, that river, though extending for a hundred yojanas, was spread on all sides with waves of fierce roaring and was deep and difficult to cross; it was terrifying with those submerged crying out "Father! Mother! Son!", and it was filled day and night with throngs of sinners standing on the banks.

It was entirely occupied by crocodiles, makaras, vajratuṇḍas, boars, and other flesh-eating aquatic creatures such as water-spiders, who were intent on constantly devouring one another. O Beloved, within its terrible whirlpools were sinners who had been released from their karma.

Surrounded on all sides by throngs of predatory beasts emerging and submerging, and by those who have reached a state of harsh misery and are being bitten, that great river is to be waded through by the four classes of living beings. O Goddess, supreme sovereign, how could virtuous yogis, men of knowledge, those devoted to their vows, the foremost of teachers, the initiated, and those who do not look upon the path of worldly time—those who do not treat with contempt their mother, their guru, their preceptor, and their father, O Mistress of the God of Gods—ever behold the Vaitaraṇī?

O beloved, one who betrays trust even while living among them, one who is intent on seeking out their faults, and one who abandons a virtuous wife shall dwell there eternally. He who approaches a weary or hungry Brahmin to create an obstacle, he who interrupts a discourse, and he who breaks up a gathering shall dwell there. A false witness, a poisoner, an arsonist, a drunkard, a slanderer, one who lives by thievery, and one who steals shall dwell there perpetually. Furthermore, one who destroys bridges or boundaries, a Brahmin who sells meat, and one who commits adultery with another's wife shall fall into the Vaitaraṇī river.

That man who, having promised to a Brahmin, does not give according to what is appropriate; he who, having invited someone, does not speak to him or let him dwell there for a long time; he who takes back a maiden already given by himself through wealth; and he who defiles a maiden—for these, residence in that [hell] is certain.

The destroyer of sacrifices, the adulterer of his master’s wife, the betrayer of friends, and one who accepts gifts in the Kali age, shall dwell for a long time in the Vaitaraṇī river. A Śūdra who drinks the milk of a Kapilā cow, a Vaiśya who recites the Vedas, a Kṣatriya who turns away from battle, and a Brāhmaṇa who abandons his private Vedic study, shall dwell for a long time in the Vaitaraṇī. One who covets another's property, one who gives with pride, one who acts in opposition to the scriptures, an ungrateful person, and a killer of a Brāhmaṇa, shall likewise dwell for a long time in the Vaitaraṇī. Should a thought ever arise in them due to the power of fortune, I shall explain the means for that [liberation]. One.

Listen to those [times], O beloved; while living, one should seek a means [to give]. At the Vyatīpāta yoga, during an eclipse, on the new moon day, on the day of a solar transit (saṅkrānti), or at any other auspicious time, one should perform this supreme gift. Or whenever faith arises toward giving, O Goddess of the Gods, that indeed shall be an auspicious time for longevity, power, and prosperity. Since these things do not remain stable forever, one should practice dharma with haste. One should respectfully present to a Brahmin a black or pinkish cow, with horns tipped in gold, hooves in silver, accompanied by a vessel of bell-metal and an offering of boiled rice.

O beautiful one, one should give to a worthy recipient a young, very auspicious cow with full udders and a calf, covered with a pair of unwashed garments and accompanied by seven types of grain, preceded by the worship of Viṣṇu, along with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) and mantras, with great reverence. O Goddess, that cow will become a divine Vaitaraṇī cow and, awaiting the donor, will come into his presence. Grasping her tail, the man shall cross the Vaitaraṇī river with ease. This same rule is prescribed even for a man who is about to die. Śrī Bhairavī said: One who accepts such a gift while still living...

"If the Brahmin has died, why does he accept that gift? Who is its witness? Tell me that. Śrī Bhairava said: "Varuṇa accepts the gift; he delivers it into the hand of Viṣṇu. And Viṣṇu, O Goddess, delivers it to the Sun (Bhāskara). From the Sun, he enjoys the fruit thereof. Thus, O Īśvarī, the resolution of your question has been declared. Now, what does your mind long to ask? [Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Recollection of the Principle of Clay," in the Śrī Bhṛṅgīśa Saṃhitā, within the dialogue between Bhairavī and Bhairava. Śrī Bhairavī said: "The six [principles] have been declared in both the Veda and the Tantra..."

O Lord, you have declared that the six duties of the twice-born—the twice-born of the first caste—are: teaching, studying, officiating at sacrifices, performing sacrifices for others, giving gifts, and receiving gifts. Yet, you have described the destiny of one who performs the act of receiving gifts as being terrible. O Lord of Gods, the rule regarding the acceptance of gifts has been prescribed specifically for the Brāhmaṇa; for other castes, however, such acceptance is considered a source of distress. In this Kali age, it is difficult to find a means of livelihood on earth for Brāhmaṇas without accepting gifts, according to what has been ordained by you. Is there some other means, O Best of Suras, by which a donor [may be helped]?

The receiver and the giver would both become partakers of merit; otherwise, the world perishes, being deprived of the donor. O Lord, you ought out of compassion to tell me this in its entirety. Śrī Bhairava said: Listen, O beautiful one, I shall speak of a most wonderful secret, knowing which nothing further remains for humans to know. O Goddess, in former times during the three ages (Yugas), all were practitioners of Dharma, with minds restrained, devoted to the contemplation of the scriptures, endowed with mental refinements such as friendliness (maitrī) and the like, having conquered their senses, and dedicated to the twilight prayers, ritual bathing, and recitation.

Those who are free from greed, performing the six duties as is appropriate and remaining detached from constant worldly actions, do not incur fault even if they take possession of the earth with its oceans and islands. In this Kali age, no one else is like Maheśāni; he who, with devotion and hospitality, worships a twice-born man with the thought that he is Maheśvara himself, is not such a person as a receiver who is possessed of all forms of greed. In the Kali age, accepting gifts is said to be equal to having seven hundred wives; therefore, O Goddess, I have refrained from accepting gifts during the Kali age. Listen now to the means [for avoiding it].

O Goddess, having performed the ritual reception (*pratigraha*) according to the rules for the *Deveśī-kalā-ghorā*, both the sage and the goddess become pure. O Goddess, since *kuśa* and *ūrvā* grass were formerly established upon the hair of Śiva and Śakti, they are therefore called "Pāvamāna" (purifying) by the wise. Therefore, a Brāhmaṇa should perform with them a purifying rite that cleanses sin, [reciting]: "O *kuśa*, you are the son of Brahmā; you are the leader of mantras, O sinless one! By my grace, may the Devas take up their residence in this *kuśa*. With this mantra, being composed, he should offer his vital breath (*prāṇa*) to it, along with the five...

O Goddess, one should worship him according to the prescribed rite; by giving a gift to him, one obtains double the fruit. O Beloved, because Śiva, joined with Śakti, is here merged within him through mantra, therefore, by worshipping him, one attains abundant enjoyments. A Kuśa-brāhmaṇa is highly commended for the ninth śrāddha, during eclipses of the moon and sun, and in other great gifts (mahādānas). Having thus performed the rite determined in the Vedas, O Mahādevī, the donor obtains double the fruit and incurs no fault. Yu—

O beloved, by improper means, even nectar becomes poison for those who drink it, and poison becomes nectar for those who consume it with proper means. If one should accept a gift from such a person out of greed or delusion, he shall suffer a loss of luster, a loss of strength, and a destruction of his merit.

"O beautiful goddess, his senses destroy him; he is not certain. One should not examine his face, O beloved, nor should one even look at him. Enough, O Great Goddess, with this much talk! In this Kali age, the acceptance of gifts must be avoided by all means.

Thus, O Goddess, has been told the determination regarding the Kuśa Brāhmaṇas, hearing which a living being is liberated from tens of millions of great sins. Śrī Bhairavī said: "The path you have described is extremely terrible, filled with great darkness; because of it, the directions are lost."

O Lord of the World, even when the *nityavartī* (daily lamp) has been offered, how great is the darkness that remains for one who departs from this world? O Master of the Universe, how can one cross the terrifying path of Yama, which is shrouded in *tāmisra* (blinding darkness), just as a cold object is warmed by heat? Śrī Bhairava said: Listen, O Goddess, as I tell you a supreme secret means for one who desires to travel upon the path of Yama, which is joined with great *tāmisra*. O Maheśvarī, on the full moon day of Kārttika, Māgha, or Phālguna, when it is conjoined with an auspicious asterism (*nakṣatra*), a favorable weekday, and an auspicious lunar day (*tithi*), [under the asterism] Dhaniṣṭhā...

O Goddess, one should avoid the five [nakṣatras], as well as Tripuṣkara—namely Bharaṇī, Kṛttikā, and Āśleṣā—and likewise the Nṛtabha; one should also avoid the sixth, Jayā, the twelfth, and Galagraha. Especially during the bright fortnight, one should avoid the days of the Moon, Mars, and Saturn.

One should perform the Dīpa-śrāddha, which dispels the darkness of the path of Yama; therein one should worship Caṇḍī, Śiva, Lakṣmī, Keśava, Rāma, Sītā, Lakṣmaṇa, and others according to the scriptures. Having lit silver lamps with golden wicks in their midst, [one should proceed].

O beloved, one should fill [the lamps] with ghee or sesame oil according to the rite; having lit the lamps, one should worship them duly with the ritual offerings (*upacāra*). With sesame seeds, cakes, meats, fish, and cooked foods, O auspicious one, I shall now declare the mantra for the offering of the lamps: "O Maheśvarī, in that world which is devoid of light, where there is neither sun nor moon—that darkness I wish to cross by means of this gift of lamps. That world of Yama, filled with great gloom, without light and without refuge—that I wish to cross by means of this gift of lamps."

O Maheśvarī, quickly destroy the mass of blinding darkness for the deceased who, being of an empty form, desires to travel the path of Yama; O Goddess whose eye is the forehead, salutations to You, who swiftly destroy the blindness of delusion for the deceased who, being of the nature of wind, desires to travel the path of Yama.

"O Great Lakṣmī, dispel the blinding darkness consisting of flames for the deceased who is being dragged along the path by the nooses of Yama as he travels; having recited this mantra, one should duly offer various lamps. Thus ends the auspicious *Mṛtisaṃdhāna*.
